objective.statement: Say whether a triad is in root position, first inversion or second inversion, from its lowest note.
successCriteria: I know the lowest note decides the position.
I know spacing and a doubled note make no difference.
I can use letters (a, b, c) or figures (5/3, 6/3, 6/4).

explanation.text: In earlier grades every triad was in root position: the root is the lowest note, and the other two notes are a 3rd and a 5th above it. This is also called a five-three chord, because of those two intervals above the bass.

A triad can be rearranged so that the 3rd or the 5th is the lowest note instead. If the 3rd is lowest, it is in first inversion (a six-three chord, written 6/3 because the other notes are a 6th and a 3rd above the lowest note). If the 5th is lowest, it is in second inversion (a six-four chord, 6/4).

music.textAlternative: Three chords of C major: C, E, G (root position); E, G, C (first inversion); G, C, E (second inversion), each from the bottom up.

explanation.caption: Chord I of C major in root position (a), first inversion (b) and second inversion (c).

explanation.text: To name a chord in a key, give its Roman numeral (the chord's root, I, IV or V) and its position. You may add a letter to the numeral: Ia, Ib, Ic. Or you may add figures: I with 5/3, 6/3 or 6/4. Both ways are accepted.

The position depends only on which note of the triad is lowest. It does not matter how far apart the upper notes are, or whether a note is doubled (written twice, an octave apart). First find the root by arranging the notes in a stack of thirds; then look at the lowest note.
Root lowest: a. Third lowest: b. Fifth lowest: c. Spacing and doubling never change the position.

music.textAlternative: A chord of G major: B, D, G from the bottom up.

steps: Stack in thirds: G B D. The root is G.
The lowest note is B, the 3rd of the chord.
So it is chord I in first inversion: Ib.
demonstration.textAlternative: A chord of G major with B lowest: Ib.

guided.prompt: In the second inversion of chord IV in D♭ major, which note is in the bass (the lowest note)?

G♭.reason: G♭ is the root of the chord, but in an inversion the root is not the lowest note.

B♭.reason: In second inversion the 5th of the chord is the lowest note.

A♭.reason: A♭ is not a note of chord IV.

hints: First inversion: the 3rd is in the bass. Second inversion: the 5th.
Second inversion: the 5th of the chord is in the bass.

mistakes.wrong-degree: Find the root: rearrange the notes into stacked 3rds — the lowest note of that stack is the root.
mistakes.root-confused-with-bass: In an inversion the lowest note is not the root: stack the notes in 3rds to find the root.
mistakes.inversion-misread: The LOWEST note decides the position: root, 3rd or 5th of the chord.
mistakes.leading-note-not-raised: In minor keys, chords use the harmonic minor, so the leading note is raised.
mistakes.note-missing: One of the notes doesn't belong. A triad has a root, a 3rd and a 5th.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Find the root first, then the bass note.
